name: Tamibarotene

lead: Tamibarotene is an oral synthetic retinoid sold in Japan as Amnolake for relapsed or refractory acute promyelocytic leukemia. It targets retinoic acid receptors alpha and beta.
It is considered more stable and potent than ATRA, and is being studied in newer trials for RARA-overexpressing blood cancers. Its link to looks comes from being a retinoid; it is not a skin product.

paras: It binds RAR-alpha and RAR-beta, nuclear receptors that control genes for cell differentiation, and spares RAR-gamma. Compared with ATRA it binds less to cellular retinoic acid binding protein, so plasma levels stay up during daily dosing.[1]

Side effects resemble other retinoids, with hyperlipidemia a common finding, and early trials suggested milder effects than ATRA.[1] It is a prescription cancer drug marketed in Japan, and retinoids as a class carry pregnancy warnings.

chain: Retinoid signalling that regulates cell differentiation
angle.text: Tamibarotene is a retinoid, the class known for skin renewal, so it appears in discussions of retinoid options. Its approved use is oral treatment of a blood cancer in Japan, and no published skin-appearance trials exist.

lead: Tamibarotene (also called Am80 or retinobenzoic acid) is a synthetic, orally taken retinoid that selectively activates retinoic acid receptors alpha and beta. It belongs to the same broad family as the retinoids people use for skin, such as tretinoin, and is of interest in skin-focused circles for that reason.[1][2]

It is approved in Japan, under the brand name Amnolake, for relapsed or refractory acute promyelocytic leukemia, and was designed to overcome limitations of all-trans retinoic acid (ATRA): it is chemically more stable, several times more potent in cell differentiation tests and keeps steadier blood levels during daily use.[1][3] It is not marketed as a cosmetic or dermatological skin product.
Research has since extended to other conditions, including myelodysplastic syndrome and acute myeloid leukemia with RARA overexpression, Alzheimer's disease models, and autoimmune diseases.[4][5][6]

paras: Tamibarotene is approved in Japan for relapsed or refractory acute promyelocytic leukemia.[1] A randomized trial found it effective as maintenance therapy in APL compared with ATRA, and its final results reported improved relapse-free survival.[7][8]
No cosmetic or dermatological formulation has been approved. Its relevance to looks comes from belonging to the retinoid class, whose members such as ATRA are used in some skin diseases.[6]
Tamibarotene is selective for RAR-alpha and RAR-beta over RAR-gamma. It is more stable than ATRA and has lower clearance, which sustains plasma levels.[1][6]
Its side effect profile is similar to that of tretinoin, with hyperlipidemia reported commonly; trials found adverse effects milder than with ATRA.[1][2]

It was originally developed by Shionogi, with input from the University of Tokyo, and was later licensed by Nippon Shinyaku from Toko Pharmaceutical for APL.[4] Later development in the US targeted RARA-overexpressing AML and higher-risk MDS under the name SY-1425.[9][10]

Phase 2 and 3 studies have examined tamibarotene with azacitidine in higher-risk MDS and with venetoclax and azacitidine in RARA-positive AML.[9][10] Preclinical work has examined Alzheimer's disease, and trials have been registered for lupus nephritis, Crohn's disease, polycystic kidney disease and heart failure.[5][11]

Human trials concern leukemia, myelodysplastic syndrome and other diseases; none concern skin appearance. In APL, tamibarotene maintenance was compared with ATRA in randomized trials and in Japan's JALSG-APL204 study it improved relapse-free survival.[7][8] Tamibarotene was also tested in steroid-refractory chronic graft-versus-host disease.[12]
